headline: The UN cannot agree on its next leader

sources.title: Latest vote shows no candidate for UN chief has the required support of all five key powers (AP)
Informal poll shows Costa Rica's Grynspan ahead in race to be next UN chief (Reuters)
Costa Rica's Grynspan extends lead in race to become next UN chief (The National)

chunks.text: On October 16, 2026, the UN Security Council held a [[secret vote]] on who should {{take over}} as the next UN leader. The current leader will {{step down}} on December 31 after two [[five-year terms]]. None of the seven candidates in the [[race]] has support from all five [[permanent members]]. These are the U.S., Russia, China, Britain and France. Each can [[veto]] a candidate.

verbs.why: An assistant coach often takes over as head coach. A new principal takes over the school in June. The council is choosing who should take over as the next leader of the UN.

verbs.wrong: To lose a vote by a little
verbs.why: Many team captains step down after ten years. Mayors step down when their terms end. The current UN leader will step down on December 31 after two five-year terms.

chunks.text: Candidates for [[secretary-general]] try to {{line up}} support among the council's 15 members. The council holds [[informal]] [[straw polls]] to {{narrow down}} the list. Members mark each candidate "encourage," "discourage" or "no opinion." On October 16, permanent members used red [[ballots]] for the first time. Candidates can now {{find out}} if a big power is against them. A winner needs nine votes [[in favor]] and no veto. Then the General Assembly {{signs off on}} the choice.

verbs.wrong: To hide your plans from others
verbs.why: Smart workers line up support from coworkers before a meeting. A politician lines up votes for his plan. Candidates try to line up support among the council's 15 members.

verbs.wrong: To sort a list by name
verbs.why: Most renters narrow down their choices to two apartments. Coaches narrow the team down to 12 players. The council holds straw polls to narrow down the list of candidates.

verbs.correct: To learn a fact you did not know
verbs.wrong: To show others what you think
verbs.why: Travelers find out about late flights from an app. Students find out their test results online. The red ballots let candidates find out if a big power is against them.
Bosses sign off on vacation days. The city council signs off on new parks. The General Assembly signs off on the council's choice for secretary-general.

chunks.text: The head of the UN's [[trade agency]], who is from Costa Rica, {{came out on top}} again. But two diplomats said she and the next two candidates each received two red "discourage" votes. The other two are Argentina's candidate, who runs the UN's [[nuclear watchdog]], and Guyana's [[ambassador]] to the UN. Two candidates from Ecuador {{ended up}} at the bottom. The job usually [[rotates]] between regions, and this is Latin America's [[turn]]. There is also pressure to choose the first woman.

verbs.wrong: To speak first at a meeting
verbs.why: Our school comes out on top in the science contest every year. In close games, the home team often comes out on top. The head of the UN's trade agency came out on top again in the October 16 poll.

verbs.correct: To finally reach a certain place
verbs.why: Lost drivers often end up on the wrong side of town. Some first books end up at the top of the best-seller list. Two candidates from Ecuador ended up at the bottom of the poll.

chunks.text: A candidate must {{win over}} the five powers or at least avoid a veto. U.S. officials say no candidate is [[ideal]] for the Trump [[administration]]. The U.S. has {{pulled out of}} some UN agencies. The U.S. ambassador said the UN needs to {{cut back}}. Still, the U.S. has not {{ruled out}} backing one of the seven. The U.S. and Russian ambassadors said new candidates could still be {{put forward}}. Both hope for a winner before the end of 2026.

verbs.wrong: To share a secret with someone
verbs.why: Kind teachers win over their classes quickly. A polite boyfriend wins over his girlfriend's parents. A candidate must win over the five powers or at least avoid a veto.

verbs.correct: To stop being part of a group
verbs.wrong: To give an award to a group
verbs.why: Some schools pull out of the soccer league when costs rise. Injured players pull out of tournaments. The United States has pulled out of some UN agencies.

verbs.correct: To do less or spend less
verbs.wrong: To make a new set of rules
verbs.why: When prices rise, families cut back. Companies cut back and hire fewer people in hard times. The ambassador from the United States said the UN needs to cut back.

verbs.correct: To say no to a possible choice
verbs.why: Coaches rarely rule out playing their best player. Many people rule out moving to a new city because of cost. Officials in the United States have not ruled out backing one of the seven candidates.

verbs.correct: To name someone for a job
verbs.wrong: To praise someone in a speech
verbs.why: Each class puts forward two students for the school council. Parties put forward their candidates for mayor in the spring. The ambassadors of the United States and Russia said new candidates could still be put forward.

mainIdea.s: The UN Security Council is choosing a new secretary-general, but no candidate yet has the support of all five veto powers. Even the top three each got two red votes against them.
mainIdea.why: None of the seven has won over all five permanent members. The leading candidate came out on top, but she still got two red votes against her.

mainIdea.s: The General Assembly is stuck after a secret vote on seven people who want to lead the UN. Its new red ballots show which of its 193 countries voted against each candidate.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the vote was held by the 15-member Security Council. Only its five permanent members used red ballots.

mainIdea.s: The UN General Assembly met in New York to talk about money problems at its agencies. Many countries promised to pay more to keep aid work in poor regions running next year.
mainIdea.why: This is a different event. The council is choosing the next secretary-general, and no candidate has been able to win over all five veto powers so far.

tf.s: The current UN leader will step down at the end of 2026.
tf.why: He will step down on December 31 after two five-year terms.

tf.s: One candidate has won over all five permanent members of the council.
tf.why: None of the seven candidates has support from all five permanent members.

tf.s: The red ballots let candidates find out if a powerful country is against them.
tf.why: The five permanent members used red ballots, so candidates can see their votes.

tf.s: The candidate from Costa Rica came out on top in the poll.
tf.why: The head of the UN's trade agency led the poll again.

tf.s: U.S. officials have ruled out backing any of the seven candidates.
tf.why: U.S. officials have not ruled out backing one of the seven, though they say none is ideal.

tf.s: The U.S. and Russia said no new candidates can join the race.
tf.why: Their ambassadors said new candidates could still be put forward.

lines.text: Did you hear the UN still can't pick its next leader?
I thought they voted on October 16.
They did, but it was a straw poll held [[behind closed doors]]. They use those to {{narrow down}} the list.
The head of the UN's trade agency. She's from Costa Rica.
Not yet. She also got two red votes from the big five powers.
Red votes? What do those mean?
This time, the five permanent members used red ballots. That way candidates can {{find out}} if a big power is against them.
And any one of the five can block her.
Right. To get the job, she has to {{win over}} all of them, or at least avoid a veto.
It is. And the next two candidates also got two red votes each.
So it's [[a toss-up]] who will {{take over}} from the current leader.
Pretty much. The U.S. hasn't {{ruled out}} backing one of them, but it says none is ideal.
Could new people still join the race?
Yes, countries can still {{put forward}} new candidates.
But the current leader will {{step down}} on December 31. They're [[cutting it close]].

expressions.def: Used to say that something happens in private, away from the public
ex: The two companies met behind closed doors.
The deal was made behind closed doors.

expressions.def: Used to say that something is completely decided and will not change
ex: The new contract is a done deal.
Don't worry about the house. It's a done deal.

expressions.def: Used to say that something will be very hard to win or do
ex: Learning a new language at 60 can be an uphill battle.

expressions.def: Used to say that two or more results are equally possible
ex: It's a toss-up whether we eat pizza or tacos tonight.
The final game is a toss-up.

expressions.def: Used to say that someone has left very little time to do something
ex: You're leaving at 7:50 for an 8:00 class? That's cutting it close.
